instruction.text: You will hear six people talking about gender quota. For each of them, decide whether they are pro or against the idea of quotas.

atoms.a: Yeah… I used to roll my eyes at quotas, honestly. But I’ve worked in two companies where the best person gets the job thing somehow always meant hiring your mate from the same old network. Once they introduced targets—call it a quota if you want—suddenly they actually looked wider, and the hires were great. It didn’t feel like lowering standards; it felt like finally applying them fairly. So yeah, I’m not in love with the word, but some kind of quota-ish push? I get it.

Where I grew up, women were literally told, This isn’t for you. So you see … that doesn’t vanish in one generation. And history shows you sometimes need a push—like, voting rights didn’t happen because society politely evolved. A quota can create role models and normalize women in power, so the next round isn’t, THE FIRST WOMAN, every time. It’s not perfect, but it’s a lever.

In my last team, we hired mostly through referrals, and surprise—referrals looked like the people already there. When we made a rule to shortlist more women, the talent pool didn’t get worse; it got better. I don’t think it’s about ‘giving women a gift.’ It’s more like correcting a tilted playing field that we pretend is flat. Long story short: I didn’t like quotas at first, but I’m kind of convinced now.

To be honest, I don't understand why we're still talking about this. Of course, men aren't evil or anything, but systems don't just correct themselves. There’s research on bias in hiring, even when people THINK they’re being objective. Quotas force institutions to notice who they’re overlooking. Ideally we wouldn’t need them, sure, but ‘ideally’ hasn’t exactly delivered so far. If a quota is what gets us to a more normal balance, I can live with it.

I understand why quotas sound tempting—fast fix, right? But once you start assigning seats by category, it gets messy. What if you’re the ‘wrong’ gender for a role, even if you’re genuinely the strongest candidate? And these policies tend to hang around. Plus companies can hit the target and still keep the old vibe, just with different faces. I’d rather see transparent criteria, structured interviews, maybe blind screening—make it about competence, not category.

It’s tricky, because I totally want more women in charge. I just hate anything that makes it feel like you’re being counted, not chosen. I’ve watched a friend get promoted and people instantly whispered: Oh, she’s the quota hire. That’s brutal! I’d rather attack the reasons women drop out—childcare, hours, the boys network’—than set a number and hope the culture follows. Numbers can solve optics — not respect.
